title: For Latino Caucus, immigrant protections are top priority: ‘We cannot afford to be silent’
summary: In 2025, the Latino Caucus backed 55 bills, 20 of which became law. This year, they are back with proposals, many of which are aimed at protecting their constituents from immigration raids that have put entire communities on edge.
content:
by Rosanne Skirble, Maryland Matters January 16, 2026

by Rosanne Skirble, Maryland Matters January 16, 2026

One recent morning, Del. Gabriel Acevero (D-Montgomery) opened his computer to an email from a desperate family:  “Please help us locate our elderly family friend who has been detained,” it read.

“This is the moment we are in right now,” says Acevero, who serves as vice chair of the Maryland Latino Legislative Caucus. “We serve as the voice of the Latino and immigrant community to assure that we are reflecting their concerns and aspirations with legislation and a budget that is fair, equitable and meets the moment.”

Acevero says the caucus can use its 91 members – the largest caucus in Annapolis – to leverage its priorities to address fears like those in that short note.

In 2025, caucus members voted to support 55 pieces of legislation. Included in the 20 that were ultimately signed into law were inclusive policies for returning citizens, anti-poverty and housing policies, health care access, child welfare and transportation safety. Some that did not succeed last year have already been reintroduced this year and pushed to the top of the caucus’ agenda.

According to a Brookings Institution report, Maryland’s Latino community had a growth spurt in 2025 attracting 32,646 new residents, adding to the approximately 800,000 already living across the state, but largely in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties.

Acevero says in 2026 the caucus is resolute in its mission to combat federal government measures that target Latinos. That focus is on immigrant protection with three key bills. One would prohibit 287(g) agreements,  the collaborative agreements between local law enforcement agencies and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). That provision was stripped from the 2025 Maryland Values Act on the last day of the 2025 session.

More than 3,300 Marylanders were detained by ICE in 2025, twice the number of preceding years

Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince Georges), who sponsored the Values Act, says she will reintroduce the 287(g) measure as a standalone bill.  “I am very optimistic that it will pass because we have really great partners in the Senate who are committed to ensuring that this bill passes this session,” she said.

Among those partners is Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City). Another is House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s), who told Maryland Matters, that she also supports the measure.

“I think it’s important, especially given the climate that we have presently in this country,” said Peña-Melnyk, a native of the Dominican Republic. “The states have to act. This is a way for us to tell our immigrant community, ‘We love you. You’re part of us. We see you. We hear you, and we want to give you protection,’ and that’s why this is important.”

Williams anticipates opposition from the Maryland counties that have signed 287(g) cooperative agreements, eight in total. Arguing for their termination, she says the stand-alone bill promotes greater trust and better relations with the police in the long run.

“We want to make sure that people feel comfortable reporting crimes to the police, engaging with our local officers, and that our officers are engaging in community policing, where the community feels as though they are part of it,” Williams said.

Two other bills among caucus priorities include House Bill 155, also drafted by Williams, which would bar on-duty law enforcement officers from wearing masks or disguises when interacting with the public. Senate Bill 1 is the companion measure in the Senate.

The other from Del. Vaughn Stewart (D-Montgomery) would bar ICE arrests in courthouses. The measure would build on the sensitive location guidelines of the Maryland Values Act that restricts federal enforcement agents from schools, churches, libraries, places of worship, hospitals, clinics and community shelters.

Among the caucus members seven are of Latino heritage – the other 84 associate members support caucus priorities.  They have crafted dozens of bills, which at their core are immigrant related, but have a broader reach. “I’m coming into this session with a pretty comprehensive agenda around affordability and workers’ rights,” said Del. Joe Vogel (D-Montgomery), whose parents brought him to the United States from Uruguay at age 3 in 2000.

Elected to the House in 2022, he is now the caucus secretary. “I spent the last nine months, both here in my district – Gaithersburg and Rockville – and then in other parts of the state hearing directly from Marylanders, from immigrants, who are really hurting now, fearful of the federal government and struggling to keep up with the rising cost of living,” he said.

Caucus Treasurer Del. Deni Taveras, a Dominican American, also has several prospective bills with immigrants in mind, ranging from developmental disability service for Latino families, an anti-price gouging housing bill, and legislation around teen pregnancy, chronic truancy and drug addiction among Latinos.

Caucus delegate Teresa Woorman (D-Montgomery) immigrated from Puebla, Mexico, as a child, became a naturalized citizen in college and served as a long-term staffer in the General Assembly before she began her first term as a legislator in 2025.

This year she strongly supports the Latino Caucus agenda, with bills of her own that include working with Peña-Melnyk to tweak a law that would put in-state tuition for undocumented students on parity with neighboring states.

She says while her constituents live in Bethesda and Potomac, areas with much less threatened by ICE,  “When I go door-knocking, people are worried about what they see on their TVs, what’s happening across the whole country,” she said.  “And I tell them I feel like we are [in Annapolis] as the first line of defense to protect what we can at the state level.”

Acevedo is ready for the fight.

“What we are seeing is a federal government that is targeting hard working Marylanders and immigrants who have come to this country and who have called this country home for decades,” he said.  “We are going to continue to push legislation, raise our voices. We are going to be in the streets shoulder to shoulder with our partners and our allies to call out this administration.  We cannot afford to be silent.”
